planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall into well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun; native terrestrial orchids like this one need specific mycorrhizal fungi already present in the soil and should never be wild-collected.

directions: Great Plains ladies' tresses grows in calcareous prairie remnants, fens, and dry-mesic grasslands from Texas north through the Dakotas and east into Ohio and Ontario, favoring drier, more alkaline soil than most other Spiranthes. It blooms in autumn, producing a single dense, tightly single-ranked spiral of white flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance that intensifies noticeably at dusk, when it is pollinated by night-flying moths and bumblebees. Unusually among orchids, most populations are apomictic, setting seed without pollination, which has allowed it to persist in isolated prairie fragments. It requires undisturbed prairie soil biology and nursery-propagated stock; do not amend the soil with fertilizer or organic matter, and never dig from the wild.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall into moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; native terrestrial orchids like this one need specific mycorrhizal fungi already present in the soil and should never be wild-collected.

directions: Giant spiral ladies' tresses is a coastal plain native found in wet pine flatwoods, savannas, and seepage slopes from North Carolina south to Florida and west to Texas, typically in fire-maintained longleaf pine habitat. It takes its name from its unusually long, curved floral lip relative to other Spiranthes, and its flower spike is among the largest and showiest of the eastern ladies' tresses, blooming from fall into early winter depending on latitude. Populations are uncommon and closely tied to periodic fire that keeps competing vegetation low. Because it depends on fire-adapted wetland soil conditions and specific fungal partners, it should only be attempted with nursery-propagated stock in a consistently moist, acidic bog garden setting; never collect from the wild.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated corms in spring into seasonally moist, sandy prairie soil in full sun; native terrestrial orchids like this one need specific mycorrhizal fungi already present in the soil and should never be wild-collected.

directions: Oklahoma grass pink grows in tallgrass and mixed-grass prairie swales and seasonally moist depressions across Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, Missouri, Kansas, and Louisiana, in soil that is damp in spring but noticeably drier by midsummer than the boggy habitat of its relative Calopogon tuberosus. It was only formally described as a distinct species in 2002, separated from C. tuberosus by its earlier spring bloom time and, unusually for the genus, its ability to self-pollinate without an insect visitor. Its magenta-pink flowers otherwise resemble other grass pinks, with the fringed, upward-facing lip that flips insects onto the pollen below. Site nursery-propagated corms in a prairie planting or seasonally moist bed that stays damp in spring and dries out by summer; do not fertilize or amend the soil.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated corms in fall into wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; native terrestrial orchids like this one need specific mycorrhizal fungi already present in the soil and should never be wild-collected.

directions: Bearded grass pink is the smallest-flowered of the eastern Calopogon species, native to wet pine savannas, flatwoods, and bog margins of the coastal plain from North Carolina south to Florida and west to Louisiana. It is also the earliest to bloom of the grass pinks, sending up its diminutive magenta flower spikes as early as February in the Deep South while most other native orchids are still dormant, arising from a single narrow, grasslike leaf. Like other Calopogon, it offers no nectar reward and relies on deceptive pollination, tricking naive bees into landing on its hinged, bristle-tipped lip and tumbling onto the pollen below. It depends on permanently wet, nutrient-poor, acidic sandy soil and fire-maintained habitat, so site nursery-propagated corms in a bog garden alongside pitcher plants, and never amend with fertilizer.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into moist, sandy soil in partial shade; native terrestrial orchids like this one need specific mycorrhizal fungi already present in the soil and should never be wild-collected.

directions: Michaux's orchid is native to moist pinelands, flatwoods, and sandy disturbed sites across the Gulf and southern Atlantic coastal plain from Florida to Texas and north to the Carolinas, extending south into Mexico and the Caribbean. Its most striking feature is an extraordinarily long, thread-like nectar spur, up to two inches long, trailing behind each greenish-white flower's three-lobed, deeply fringed lip; the spur length restricts pollination to long-tongued hawkmoths that visit at dusk and after dark. Flower spikes appear in late summer into fall, well after most spring-blooming native orchids have finished. Because it grows from tubers that persist through a dry dormant season, plant nursery-propagated stock in well-drained but seasonally moist sandy soil in a lightly shaded bed, and never collect from the wild.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)
